meta.notes: Buckets from the series' verified choice-state list (TX + CT, ME, MA, NH, RI, NY, NJ, PA, MD, DE, OH, IL + DC). Notes marked verify:true need a fact-check pass before launch. Ramp validated on the sage surface: choice #1d6e56, hybrid #8bb296, monopoly = neutral #d8dbc9 (same convention as No RTO: pale means nothing to choose).

choice.label: Broad choice
choice.body: Most households can choose an electricity seller. The local wires still belong to one utility, and state regulators approve its delivery prices.

hybrid.label: Limited choice
hybrid.body: Some customers can choose an electricity seller. State law limits who qualifies or how many may leave the local utility.

monopoly.label: One seller
monopoly.body: Most households buy electricity from the local utility. State regulators approve its prices.

TX.note: Most households in ERCOT can choose an electricity seller. Co-op and city-utility territories usually keep one seller. The parts of Texas outside ERCOT also have one seller.

MD.note: A 2024 law capped prices and added limits for electricity sellers. Most sellers stopped offering household plans. Part of the law remains in court.

MI.note: Michigan allows customers representing up to 10% of a utility's electricity demand to switch sellers. The limit is full, and more customers are waiting.

CA.note: California opened retail electricity sales in the 1990s and restricted them after the 2000 crisis. Many communities now choose an electricity seller on behalf of residents.

NE.note: Nebraska is the only state where every utility is owned by the public.

NV.note: Large businesses can pay a fee to leave the local utility and buy electricity elsewhere. Households cannot.

MT.note: Montana opened retail electricity sales in the 1990s. The state returned households to local utility service in 2007.

OR.note: The largest business customers can choose a seller. Households cannot.

VA.note: State law allows choice for some 100% renewable plans. Utility green plans prevent most households from qualifying. Only the largest electricity users can still choose a seller.
